newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ SPORT - Davis key to NZ's one-day series hopes.
newsitem.headline: NZ SPORT - Davis key to NZ's one-day series hopes.

text.p: NAPIER, March 21 - Wellington fast bowler Heath Davis looms as an important figure for New Zealand when they take on World Cup holders Sri Lanka in the opening match of the one-day series in Auckland on Saturday.
Davis has been identified by New Zealand coach Steve Rixon and Central Districts coach Scott Briasco as an influential player heading into the first game in the three-match series at Eden Park.

Briasco's team yesterday lacked a bowler of Davis' pace and accuracy to trouble the tourists when Sri Lanka strolled to a comfortable six-wicket win in a day-night limited-overs match against Central Districts at McLean Park in Napier.

An unbroken fifth-wicket stand of 150 from 195 balls between skipper Arjuna Ranatunga, who finished unbeaten on 96, and Hashan Tillekaratne, with 47 not out, lifted Sri Lanka to victory in 43.3 overs after their side had lost a little poise in falling to 78 for four in pursuit of Central Districts' 227.

Sri Lanka's early runs came in a torrent, with Ranatunga and Tillekaratne joining forces in just the 12th over after Aravinda de Silva, who made a cameo 34 from 25 balls, and Romesh Kaluwitharana, with 21 from just 13 deliveries, had provided the early fireworks.
But Central Districts lacked the penetration to trouble the world one-day champions, a quality Briasco said Davis possessed.

"Heath Davis will give them a hurry-up. He's been bowling very straight and whacking it in, and I don't think the Sri Lankan batsmen fancy the ball coming at them too quickly," he told NZPA after the tourists got their tour back on track after
heavy defeats in both of the two test matches against New Zealand.
"Their batting lineup is a scary factor, and if one or two in their top order come off the Sri Lankans will be in a position to defend a big score.
"They are a completely different team in the one-day arena compared to tests, but the same principles apply," Briasco said.
"They don't like it if you bowl straight and tuck their batsmen up. I think the New Zealand attack should be quite useful in terms of countering the Sri Lankans' strengths.
"But if you give them anything loose, they are going to whack it, and their batsmen place the ball so well."

Davis, who battled knee and achilles tendon problems throughout the two tests, is expected to be fit for tomorrow's game, and his value to the Kiwi side was amplified when Rixon said he wanted to use tactics similar to those employed in Sharjah last November when New Zealand tackled Sri Lanka head-on during a triangular one-day tournament there.

The New Zealand new-ball bowlers were instructed to attack the Sri Lankan top order in Sharjah, and that policy rewarded the Kiwis with one win and one tied result against a side whose frenetic approach during the early overs in their glorious World Cup campaign 12 months ago revolutionised the way teams approached limited-overs matches.
"Heath is our strike bowler, and the philosophy of taking it to the Sri Lankans -- as we did in Sharjah -- is one we want to take into this game," Rixon told NZPA.
"In that case it is important that Heath plays."
New Zealand squad member Andrew Penn gained invaluable first-hand experience against the tourists yesterday, and emerged from his first match in more than three weeks a lot wiser for the exposure.

Penn has been included in the New Zealand one-day squad for the first time after performing 12th-man duties during the second test in Hamilton earlier this week, but he is not expected to play in Auckland unless Davis is ruled out because of fitness worries.

Despite conceding 47 runs from just nine overs, Penn felt he was in better shape to confront the Sri Lankans at some stage during the series than he would have been without the benefit of yesterday's match behind him.
"The margin for error is just that much smaller against them than it is in domestic first-class or Shell Cup level," Penn said.
"Against someone like Aravinda de Silva you just have to bowl that much straighter and fuller, and give the ball as much chance as possible to swing.
"As soon as you give him any width the ball is gone through the covers. He is a difficult man to bowl to."

De Silva, who had a wretched time in the test series when four visits to the crease rewarded him with just nine runs, looked to be hitting his straps again against Central Districts when he helped himself to six fours and one six in 36 minutes before he miscued against innocuous medium pacer Brent Williams to gift Penn an easy catch at point.
Ranatunga then took centre stage, nonchalantly milking the Central bowlers and punishing anything remotely off line.
Briasco thinks his team may have done New Zealand a disservice in one respect.
"There was always an air of inevitability about the result here from the 25th over on. They are an international side, and we played a few of their batsmen back into form."
Teams:-

New Zealand (from): Stephen Fleming (captain), Bryan Young, Nathan Astle, Matt Horne, Chris Cairns, Adam Parore, Chris Harris, Dipak Patel, Gavin Larsen, Simon Doull, Heath Davis, Andrew Penn and Daniel Vettori.

Sri Lanka (from): Arjuna Ranatunga (captain), Sanath Jayasuriya, Romesh Kaluwitharana, Roshan Mahanama, Marvan Atapattu, Aravinda de Silva, Hashan Tillekaratne, Upul Chandana, Chaminda Vaas, Kumar Dharmasena, Sajeewa de Silva, Muttiah Muralitharan, Nuwan Zoysa, Ruwan Kalpage and Ravindra Pushpakumara.
